clue.text: Hate to say I'm in disarray

indicators.note: something in disarray is jumbled and untidy, so the preceding words are thrown out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written, doing double duty with the indicator phrase

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they hate admitting their life is a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'in' is both the last letters of the fodder and the start of the signal 'in disarray'.
explanation.definitionFit: Animosity is strong hostility or ill will, a close synonym of hatred.

clue.text: Victory was doubly his

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who won twice over
setter's reading: HMS Victory was the admiral's flagship, and he also won the victory at Trafalgar

explanation.walkthrough: Victory is both the name of a famous British warship and a win in battle; one admiral owned both at Trafalgar in 1805.
explanation.definitionFit: The admiral commanded the flagship HMS Victory and won the Battle of Trafalgar aboard her, so both senses belong to him.

clue.text: Brood about one's ill-treatment

indicators.note: about means going around, so one word is wrapped round the other

blocks.note: to muse is to brood or ponder
one's read as 'one is', I being one

explanation.surface: Someone sulks over the bad treatment they have received.
explanation.definitionFit: Misuse means treating something or someone wrongly or harmfully, which is abuse or ill-treatment.

clue.text: Guard dog - watch out!

indicators.note: out suggests standing outside, so one word sits on the outside of the other

blocks.note: to watch is to see
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A warning sign about a guard dog: beware!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch out!' reads as a warning, but 'watch' gives the outer letters and 'out' places them around the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: To secure a place is to make it safe, which is what guarding does.

clue.text: Cultivation that's up to date

blocks.note: till means until, up to
a date or period of time, an age

explanation.surface: Modern farming methods that are fully up to date.
explanation.definitionFit: Tillage is the preparation and working of land for crops, which is cultivation.

clue.text: Possibility of excellent rise in strong pound

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from the bottom upwards
in places the risen word inside the other letters

blocks.note: potent means strong
L is the abbreviation for a pound (libra)
A1 means excellent, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: An economist hopes for a sharp rise in a strong pound sterling.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is a British label for first-class quality, with the digit 1 read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Potential is latent capacity, the possibility of becoming or achieving something.

clue.text: Period given to RN formation to enter battle

indicators.note: a formation is an arrangement, so the letters are arranged afresh
entering means going inside, so the rearranged letters go within the other word

blocks.note: a battle is a fight
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spell of time allotted to a Royal Navy fleet formation going into battle.
explanation.walkthrough: RN is the Royal Navy. The rearranged letters sit after the first letter of the battle word.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortnight is a period of two weeks, a specific span of time.

clue.text: Clerk gives pound to drug peddler

blocks.note: a pound is an enclosure for animals, a pen
a pusher sells illegal drugs

explanation.surface: An office clerk passes money to a drug dealer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like money, but here it is an animal enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen-pusher is a disparaging term for an office worker doing dull paperwork, a clerk.

clue.text: "Moody" could describe Romeo's disposition

indicators.note: disposition can mean arrangement, so the letters are disposed in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Romeo was a sulky, moody young man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposition' seems to mean temperament, which fits the surface, but it signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Morose means sullen and gloomy in temper, which is a moody state.

clue.text: End with a shout and a squeak

blocks.note: the close is the end
a shout is a call; 'with' adds it on

explanation.surface: Something finishes with a yell and a squeak, like a frightened animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A squeak' is short for a narrow squeak, a lucky escape.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow squeak and a close call both mean a near miss, an escape from danger by a tiny margin.

clue.text: Sensible car drivers do keep quiet

blocks.note: first meaning: fasten their seat belts
second meaning: a rude command to stop talking

explanation.surface: Good drivers concentrate on the road and don't chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is British slang, a blunt way of saying 'shut up'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both buckling a seat belt and, as slang, falling silent.

clue.text: The nearest way to the sea

definitions.text: The nearest way to the sea

blocks.clueFragment: The nearest way to the sea
blocks.note: surface reading: the quickest route down to the beach
setter's reading: the route that runs closest alongside the sea, a road following the shore

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearest way' seems to mean the shortest route, but it means the route lying nearest the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A road running along the shoreline is the highway physically closest to the sea.

clue.text: Steps inside

blocks.note: surface reading: an invitation to come in
setter's reading: a noun, a flight of steps indoors

explanation.walkthrough: 'Steps inside' reads as a verb phrase, someone entering; read as a noun phrase it is indoor steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A staircase is a set of steps within a building, as opposed to outdoor steps.

clue.text: Stubborn stain to be treated

indicators.note: something treated is processed or worked on, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stubborn stain on fabric that needs treating.
explanation.definitionFit: Obstinate means refusing to change one's mind, a direct synonym of stubborn.

clue.text: Film sponsor

blocks.note: first meaning: Coppola's 1972 Mafia film
second meaning: a man who sponsors a child at baptism

explanation.walkthrough: A sponsor at a christening promises to support the child's religious upbringing.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the famous gangster movie, and the male baptismal sponsor of a child.

clue.text: Try to reach agreement, but get into a difficulty over one point

indicators.note: being in difficulty suggests trouble and disorder, so the letters are muddled

blocks.note: taken as written
E is one point of the compass, east

explanation.surface: Negotiators trying to settle hit a snag over one particular point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get into a difficulty' reads as a phrase, but 'difficulty' is the signal for the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To negotiate is to discuss terms with others in order to reach a settlement.

clue.text: Ready for collection

blocks.note: first meaning: prepared
second meaning: a group of things that belong together

explanation.surface: Something waiting to be picked up.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means prepared to go, and also a matching group such as a set of chairs.

clue.text: A well-endowed result

blocks.note: surface reading: a richly funded or generous outcome
setter's reading: a place blessed with a well, a mineral spring, and the resort that grows from it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-endowed' suggests wealth; here it means gifted with a well of mineral water.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort town grows up around a mineral spring, so it is what results from having such a well.

clue.text: Fix a result

blocks.note: first meaning: to fasten or bind
second meaning: a drawn match, where scores are level

explanation.surface: Rigging the outcome of a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix a result' suggests match-fixing, but it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to fasten with a knot, and a match ending level is this kind of outcome.

clue.text: Disapproval, we hear, increasing for drinking spree

indicators.note: we hear says the preceding word is judged by its sound, not spelling

blocks.note: boos are jeers of disapproval
going up means increasing

explanation.surface: Mounting public disapproval of a binge-drinking session.
explanation.definitionFit: A booze-up is a British colloquial term for a heavy drinking party or session.

clue.text: Have I no novel written by Sir Walter Scott?

definitions.note: short for a novel written by him

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they lack a Walter Scott novel on their shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' does double duty: it signals the rearrangement and hints at the book.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivanhoe is Scott's 1819 historical romance of medieval England, his best-known book.

clue.text: A church service

blocks.note: taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A religious service held in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' looks like worship, but it is a tennis serve.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, a serve the opponent cannot touch is an unreturnable winning service.

clue.text: It gives a lift when a flier goes over an obstacle

blocks.note: a crow is a bird, a flier
a bar is a barrier or obstacle

explanation.surface: A bird gets an updraft as it flies over a barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'goes over' places the first piece on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: This iron lever is used to prise and raise heavy things, so it lifts them.

clue.text: It protects pans cook left on

indicators.note: to cook something can mean to doctor or falsify it, so the letters are tampered with

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A non-stick coating saves pans even when the cook leaves them on the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like the person at the stove; it is a verb meaning to tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: This brand-name non-stick coating lines frying pans so food does not burn onto them.

clue.text: Something very enjoyable is still second best

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
the cream is the best part

explanation.surface: A fun experience is still not quite the best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second best' reads as a phrase meaning runner-up, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, a hilarious or highly entertaining thing is called a scream, as in 'the party was a scream'.

clue.text: Scolded for raising details I left out

indicators.note: something left out is omitted, so that letter is dropped
in a down entry, raising lifts the word so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letter to remove

explanation.surface: Someone was told off for bringing up particulars but omitting their own part.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from the plural word, then read the rest upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To slate someone is British informal for criticising them severely, so it means scolded.

clue.text: Rush through a life's work

blocks.note: first meaning: to move headlong and out of control
second meaning: a profession followed over one's working years

explanation.surface: Someone hurries through their whole working life.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to hurtle along wildly; as a noun it is one's chosen occupation over a lifetime.

clue.text: It takes the lead

blocks.note: surface reading: something that goes first or is in charge
setter's reading: a leash clipped onto a pet's neck band

explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the lead' means goes in front; here it means the leash is attached to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A band worn round a pet's neck has a ring to which the leash is fastened.

clue.text: A complete fool can be turned to a humorist

indicators.note: being turned round means read the word back to front

blocks.note: a can is a tin
a wit is a clever, funny person

explanation.surface: An utter idiot can become a comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the verb; it is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitwit is a silly, stupid person, an informal word for a fool.

clue.text: The more there are, the fewer there are

definitions.text: The more there are, the fewer there are

blocks.clueFragment: The more there are, the fewer there are
blocks.note: surface reading: an apparent paradox
setter's reading: each extra missing person means one fewer person present

explanation.walkthrough: The riddle resolves when 'there are' means 'are present': the more people missing, the smaller the attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: People who are away from a meeting or class reduce the number in attendance as their count grows.

clue.text: Break for food in attempt to reach agreement

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other

blocks.note: an attempt is a try
to stop to have a meal, to eat

explanation.surface: Negotiators pause for a meal while trying to strike a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty is a formal agreement between states, a signed accord.

clue.text: One of the odder army varieties of transport

definitions.text: One of the odder army varieties of transport

indicators.note: varieties suggests different forms, so the letters take a different form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A curious form of military transport.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: camel corps used these animals, an odd kind of army transport.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-humped camel served as a mount for desert troops such as camel corps, an unusual military conveyance.
